title: The Cardiac Cycle and Pressure-Volume Loops

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: What single rule decides when a heart valve opens and when it shuts?
cards.back: A valve opens when the pressure behind it exceeds the pressure ahead, and shuts when that reverses.
cards.quote: A valve opens when the pressure behind it exceeds the pressure ahead, and shuts when that reverses.
cards.section: One beat, four valve events

cards.front: In the adult human left heart at rest, the aortic valve opens when LV pressure reaches about 80 mmHg. Whose pressure is that 80 mmHg, and why does it set the opening point?
cards.back: It is the aorta's diastolic pressure, not the ventricle's. The valve opens only once LV pressure rises above the pressure ahead of it in the aorta.
cards.quote: The 80 mmHg is the aorta's diastolic pressure, not the ventricle's.
cards.section: One beat, four valve events

cards.front: Diastole of the left ventricle runs from aortic closure to mitral closure. What are its three main parts?
cards.back: Isovolumic relaxation, early filling and atrial contraction.
cards.quote: It has three main parts: isovolumic relaxation, early filling and atrial contraction.
cards.section: One beat, four valve events

cards.front: On a Wiggers diagram, the ECG's QRS complex comes just before {{c1::mitral closure}}.
cards.back: The P wave comes just before atrial contraction; the T wave around the end of ejection.
cards.quote: The ECG's P wave comes just before atrial contraction, the QRS complex just before mitral closure, and the T wave around the end of ejection
cards.section: One beat, four valve events

cards.front: On a left-ventricular pressure-volume loop, why are the right and left sides vertical lines?
cards.back: On each, both valves are shut, so no blood can enter or leave and volume cannot change while pressure rises or falls: the two isovolumic phases.
cards.quote: On each, both valves are shut, so no blood can enter or leave and the volume cannot change while the pressure rises or falls.
cards.section: Fold time away and the beat becomes a loop

cards.front: Name the valve event at each corner of a left-ventricular pressure-volume loop (counterclockwise from bottom right).
cards.back: Bottom right: mitral closes (EDV, S1). Top right: aortic opens. Top left: aortic closes (ESV and Pes, S2). Bottom left: mitral opens.
cards.quote: bottom right is mitral closure at end-diastolic volume (EDV); the right side is isovolumic contraction; top right is aortic opening; the top is ejection.
cards.section: Fold time away and the beat becomes a loop

cards.front: On a left-ventricular pressure-volume loop, stroke volume (EDV − ESV) is the loop's {{c1::width}}.
cards.quote: Stroke volume, SV = EDV - ESV: the loop's width.
cards.section: Fold time away and the beat becomes a loop

cards.front: On a left-ventricular pressure-volume loop, stroke work (about SV x mean ejection pressure) is the loop's {{c1::area}}.
cards.quote: How much work does one beat do? Stroke work, SW ≈ SV x mean ejection pressure: the loop's area, approximated as a rectangle.
cards.section: Fold time away and the beat becomes a loop

cards.front: A model adult left ventricle has EDV 140 mL and ESV 56 mL at a heart rate of 75 per min. Find stroke volume, ejection fraction and cardiac output.
cards.back: SV = 140 - 56 = 84 mL. EF = 84 / 140 = 60 percent. CO = 84 mL x 75 per min = 6.3 L per min.
cards.quote: Cardiac output, CO = SV x HR, with HR the heart rate in beats per min.
cards.section: Fold time away and the beat becomes a loop

cards.front: A model left ventricle ejects 70 mL; the aortic valve opens at 80 mmHg and end-systolic pressure is 110 mmHg. Taking mean ejection pressure as the average of the two, estimate stroke work in mmHg mL and in joules.
cards.back: Mean pressure (80 + 110) / 2 = 95 mmHg. SW = 70 x 95 = 6,650 mmHg mL. x 1.333 x 10^-4 J per mmHg mL = about 0.89 J per beat.
cards.section: Worked problem, part 1: read one loop

cards.front: In the two-line model of a left-ventricular beat, where does each steady beat end, and what are the two lines?
cards.back: At the one point where two lines cross: the ventricle's ESPVR (rising right from V0, slope Ees) and the arteries' line (climbing left from EDV, steepness Ea). Opposite slopes cross exactly once.
cards.quote: Every beat ends where two lines cross.
cards.section: Worked problem, part 1: read one loop

cards.front: What does the end-systolic pressure-volume relation (ESPVR) of the left ventricle describe, and what does its slope Ees index?
cards.back: How much pressure the fully contracted ventricle holds at each volume. Its slope Ees, an elastance (pressure change per volume change), tracks contractility.
cards.quote: It says how much pressure the fully contracted ventricle holds at each volume.
cards.section: The ventricle's line: a stiff line at end-systole, a soft curve at end-diastole

cards.front: In canine hearts, a balloon briefly occludes the inferior vena cava, so over a few beats the left ventricle fills less and its pressure-volume loops shrink and move left. What do the loops' end-systolic corners show?
cards.back: They fall on one near-linear line, the ESPVR, relatively insensitive to loading.
cards.why: Varying filling samples many points on the same ventricular line, so its slope Ees and intercept V0 can be fitted.
cards.quote: Suga, Sagawa and colleagues reported in canine hearts that the end-systolic points of differently loaded beats fall on one near-linear line, relatively insensitive to loading.
cards.section: The ventricle's line: a stiff line at end-systole, a soft curve at end-diastole

cards.front: A model left ventricle has a linear ESPVR with V0 = 10 mL and Ees = 2.5 mmHg per mL. A beat ends at an end-systolic pressure of 110 mmHg. What is its end-systolic volume?
cards.quote: Run it backwards to find the volume for a given pressure: ESV = V0 + Pes / Ees = 5 + 120 / 3.0 = 45 mL.
cards.section: The ventricle's line: a stiff line at end-systole, a soft curve at end-diastole

cards.front: What raises and what lowers Ees, the slope of the left ventricle's ESPVR?
cards.back: Raised by positive inotropes and sympathetic activation; lowered by ischaemia and infarction.
cards.quote: Ees rises with positive inotropes (drugs that strengthen contraction) and sympathetic activation and falls with ischaemia and infarction.
cards.section: The ventricle's line: a stiff line at end-systole, a soft curve at end-diastole

cards.front: Why can a rise in Ees not always be read as stronger heart muscle?
cards.back: Ees is a chamber-level index, so wall geometry and passive stiffness affect it too: in a stiff, thick-walled chamber Ees can rise without stronger muscle.
cards.quote: in a stiff, thick-walled chamber Ees can rise without stronger muscle.
cards.section: The ventricle's line: a stiff line at end-systole, a soft curve at end-diastole

cards.front: The slope of the end-diastolic pressure-volume relation indexes chamber stiffness; its inverse, volume change per unit pressure, is {{c1::compliance}}.
cards.quote: its slope indexes chamber stiffness, and the inverse is compliance, volume change per unit pressure.
cards.section: The ventricle's line: a stiff line at end-systole, a soft curve at end-diastole

cards.front: At a fixed heart rate and resistance, why does end-systolic pressure rise roughly in proportion to stroke volume over many steady beats?
cards.back: Whatever is ejected each beat must run off through the arterioles before the next beat, and the pressure driving that runoff rises with the amount pumped. Pes ≈ Ea x SV.
cards.quote: Whatever the ventricle ejects each beat must run off through the arterioles before the next beat, and the pressure that drives that runoff rises with the amount pumped.
cards.section: The arteries draw the second line

cards.front: Effective arterial elastance (Ea) rises mostly with arteriolar resistance. Why does it also rise with heart rate?
cards.back: A faster heart leaves less time for blood to run off between beats, so more pressure is left per millilitre ejected.
cards.why: A common approximation is Ea ≈ R / T, total peripheral resistance over the duration of one beat.
cards.quote: also with heart rate, because a faster heart leaves less time for blood to run off between beats
cards.section: The arteries draw the second line

cards.front: Solving for the crossing of the ESPVR and the arterial line gives SV = (EDV − V0) / {{c1::(1 + Ea / Ees)}}.
cards.back: Ea/Ees is the ventricular-arterial coupling, reported near 0.6 in humans at rest.
cards.quote: SV = (EDV − V0) / (1 + Ea / Ees).
cards.section: The arteries draw the second line

cards.front: A model left ventricle has EDV 110 mL, V0 10 mL, Ees 2.5 mmHg per mL and Ea 1.25 mmHg per mL, at steady state with a linear ESPVR. Find stroke volume, end-systolic pressure and end-systolic volume.
cards.quote: Solve for the crossing and you get the stroke volume:
cards.section: The arteries draw the second line

cards.front: Model left ventricle: EDV 125 mL, V0 5 mL, Ees 3.0 and Ea 1.5 mmHg per mL (SV 80 mL, ESV 45 mL, Pes 120 mmHg). Arteriolar constriction raises Ea to 2.0 with EDV and Ees fixed. Which line moves, and what happens to the end-systolic corner, SV and EF?
cards.back: The arteries' line tilts steeper and meets the same ESPVR higher up: corner moves up and right. Pes 144 mmHg, ESV 53 mL, SV 72 mL, EF 57.6 percent.
cards.quote: The arteries' line tilts steeper and meets the same ventricle's line higher up
cards.section: Worked problem, part 2: one change at a time

cards.front: Model left ventricle: EDV 125 mL, V0 5 mL, Ees 3.0 and Ea 1.5 mmHg per mL (SV 80 mL, ESV 45 mL). Preload rises: EDV goes to 140 mL with Ea and Ees fixed. Why does stroke volume rise by less than the 15 mL rise in EDV?
cards.back: SV rises only to 90 mL: the arteries' line starts further right, so the corner slides up the same ESPVR. Pes rises to 135 mmHg, so ESV also rises, from 45 to 50 mL.
cards.quote: stroke volume rose by 10 mL, less than the 15 mL rise in EDV, because Pes rose too, so ESV rose from 45 to 50 mL.
cards.section: Worked problem, part 2: one change at a time

cards.front: Model left ventricle: EDV 125 mL, V0 5 mL, Ees 3.0 and Ea 1.5 mmHg per mL (SV 80 mL, ESV 45 mL, EF 64 percent). A positive inotrope raises Ees to 4.5 with EDV and Ea fixed. Which line moves, and what happens to ESV, SV and EF?
cards.back: The ventricle's line tilts steeper; the corner swings left along the arteries' line. ESV 35 mL, SV 90 mL, Pes 135 mmHg, EF 72 percent.
cards.quote: The ventricle's line tilts steeper: SV = 120 / 1.333 = 90 mL; Pes = 135 mmHg; ESV = 35 mL; EF = 72 percent.
cards.section: Worked problem, part 2: one change at a time

cards.front: Many textbook drawings show a preload increase with end-systolic volume unchanged, while the two-line model shows ESV rising. Why do they differ?
cards.back: The drawings hold Pes fixed; the model holds Ea fixed, so Pes rises with stroke volume and ESV climbs the ESPVR. Both are right under their own assumption.
cards.quote: Many textbook drawings keep ESV fixed instead, because they hold Pes fixed; only at fixed Pes would stroke volume rise by the full 15 mL.
cards.section: Worked problem, part 2: one change at a time

cards.front: Model left ventricle: EDV 125 mL, V0 5 mL, Ees 3.0 mmHg per mL. Ea rises from 1.5 to 2.0 and stays there, while the same 80 mL flows in each beat on top of whatever was left behind. Predict the new steady EDV, SV and Pes.
cards.back: SV returns to 80 mL at Pes = 2.0 x 80 = 160 mmHg; ESV = 5 + 160 / 3.0 ≈ 58 mL, so EDV settles near 138 mL.
cards.why: Leftover blood adds to the next fill (preload rises), so the first-beat fall in SV partly reverses within a few beats.
cards.quote: In an intact heart the blood left behind adds to the next fill, so stroke volume partly recovers within a few beats.
cards.section: Worked problem, part 2: one change at a time

cards.front: In the two-line model of the left ventricle, with Ea and Ees fixed, why does a change in preload barely change ejection fraction?
cards.back: EF = (1 − V0/EDV) / (1 + Ea/Ees). With the ratio fixed, EDV enters only through V0/EDV, which is small: 63.3 to 64.8 percent as EDV goes from 100 to 180 mL in the model.
cards.quote: At fixed Ea and Ees, preload barely touches EF
cards.section: Ejection fraction is not contractility

cards.front: Two model left ventricles both fill to 125 mL with V0 5 mL. Heart A has Ees 2.0 and Ea 1.0 mmHg per mL; heart B has Ees 4.0 and Ea 2.0. Which has the higher ejection fraction, and does that tell you which muscle is stronger?
cards.back: Neither: both have Ea/Ees = 0.5, so both eject 80 mL with EF 64 percent. Heart B ends systole at 160 mmHg, heart A at 80; B's loop is twice as tall.
cards.why: EF reads the ratio of the two slopes, not contractility.
cards.quote: EF saw the ratio, not the muscle.
cards.section: Ejection fraction is not contractility

cards.front: A dilated left ventricle has V0 40 mL, Ees 1 and Ea 2 mmHg per mL, and EDV 250 mL. Compare the exact EF with the short form 1 / (1 + Ea/Ees).
cards.back: Exact: (1 − 40/250) / (1 + 2) = 0.84 / 3 = 28 percent. Short form: 1 / 3 = 33 percent, which overstates EF because V0 is not small next to EDV.
cards.quote: In a dilated heart with V0 = 40 mL, Ees 1 and Ea 2 mmHg per mL, it gives 33 percent
cards.section: Ejection fraction is not contractility

cards.front: In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, how do the pressure-volume loop and the ventricle's lines change?
cards.back: Remodelling shifts the ESPVR, EDPVR and loops right, and the ESPVR is usually flatter (lower Ees): a large chamber ejecting a small fraction of its volume.
cards.quote: remodelling shifts the ESPVR, the EDPVR and the loops to the right, and the ESPVR is usually flatter (lower Ees)
cards.section: Loops in disease: which line has moved?

cards.front: In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, which part of the pressure-volume plot moves, and how?
cards.back: The floor: the diastolic relation (EDPVR) shifts up and left, with higher passive stiffness and a longer tau (slower relaxation).
cards.quote: Catheter studies found the diastolic relation shifted up and to the left, with higher passive stiffness and a longer tau.
cards.section: Loops in disease: which line has moved?

cards.front: In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, Ees and Ea tend to rise together. Using the two-line model, predict EF and explain why a raised Ees here does not establish healthy muscle.
cards.back: If the ratio Ea/Ees is unchanged, the model gives a similar, about normal EF. Ees is a chamber index, so a stiff chamber can raise it (as in a small catheter study); an echo-Doppler sample found depressed chamber and myocardial contractility despite raised Ees.
cards.quote: Ees was raised too in a small catheter study, and Ea and Ees tend to rise together.
cards.section: Loops in disease: which line has moved?

cards.front: Conductance-catheter loops were recorded in people with heart failure and normal EF and in controls, at baseline, during isometric handgrip (raising afterload) and during atrial pacing at 120 per min. Diastolic stiffness was raised at baseline; with pacing, stroke volume fell; with handgrip, end-diastolic pressure rose more. What do the results rule in, and what do they not show?
cards.back: Ruled in: a stiff chamber, with filling pressure rising more under load and stroke volume falling with pacing. Not shown: that stiffness is the cause, that lowering it would help, or that systolic and vascular changes are absent.
cards.quote: Diastolic stiffness was raised at baseline; with pacing, stroke volume fell and the loops shifted left; with handgrip, end-diastolic pressures rose more.
cards.section: Loops in disease: which line has moved?

cards.front: Predict how aortic stenosis changes the left-ventricular pressure-volume loop, and what happens to Ea calculated from LV pressure.
cards.back: LV systolic pressure rises and the loop's top domes upward; EDV stays near normal and ESV is often larger. Ea from LV pressure includes the valve, so Ea/Ees rises.
cards.why: The narrowed valve adds to afterload. In compensated stenosis a thickened wall can keep ESV and EF near normal.
cards.quote: In aortic stenosis the valve adds to afterload: LV systolic pressure rises and the loop's top domes upward.
cards.section: Loops in disease: which line has moved?

cards.front: In mitral stenosis, left-ventricular {{c1::preload}} falls and pulmonary venous pressure rises, while the ESPVR is usually preserved.
cards.quote: In mitral stenosis preload falls and pulmonary venous pressure rises, while the ESPVR is usually preserved (relaxation can be slowed too).
cards.section: Loops in disease: which line has moved?

cards.front: In chronic mitral regurgitation the left ventricle's muscle is damaged, but it can now eject into the low-pressure atrium as well as the aorta. Predict ejection fraction and forward output, and say why EF misleads.
cards.back: EF stays normal or supernormal while forward output is normal or reduced. Early on the low-pressure outlet helps the ventricle empty; later the dilated chamber's large EDV keeps total stroke volume high, so EF overstates the muscle.
cards.quote: So EF can stay normal or supernormal while the myocardium is damaged and forward output is normal or reduced.
cards.section: Loops in disease: which line has moved?

cards.front: A left ventricle with a mitral leak shows EDV 170 mL and ESV 60 mL on its loops, while an aortic flow probe measures 70 mL per beat. Find total stroke volume, regurgitant volume and EF, and compare EF with forward output.
cards.back: Total SV = 170 - 60 = 110 mL; regurgitant volume = 110 - 70 = 40 mL. EF = 110 / 170 = 65 percent, though only 70 mL (41 percent of EDV) goes forward.
cards.quote: A leaking mitral valve gives the systolic ventricle two outlets, the aorta and the low-pressure left atrium, so Pes / SV includes the leak.
cards.section: Loops in disease: which line has moved?

cards.front: The pressure-volume area (PVA) is stroke work plus the end-systolic {{c1::potential energy}}, elastic energy held in the contracted wall that the beat pays for but never delivers to the blood.
cards.quote: The pressure-volume area (PVA) is stroke work plus the end-systolic potential energy: elastic energy held in the contracted wall at end-systole
cards.section: What a beat costs

cards.front: In excised, cross-circulated dog hearts, oxygen use per beat rose linearly with pressure-volume area (PVA). What does this show about an isovolumic beat, which does no external work?
cards.back: It still costs oxygen in proportion to its PVA, so stroke work alone is not the cost of a beat.
cards.quote: So an isovolumic beat, which does no external work, still costs oxygen in proportion to its PVA; stroke work alone is not the cost.
cards.section: What a beat costs

cards.front: A beat has stroke work 7,000 mmHg mL, ESV 50 mL, V0 10 mL and Pes 100 mmHg. Treating potential energy as a triangle, find PVA and the oxygen use from the dog fit MVO2 ≈ 1.5 x 10^-5 x PVA + 0.019 (mL O2 per beat).
cards.back: PE = 0.5 x (50 - 10) x 100 = 2,000 mmHg mL; PVA = 9,000 mmHg mL. MVO2 = 0.135 + 0.019 = 0.154 mL O2 per beat (form only, not a human prediction).
cards.quote: treating potential energy as a triangle, 0.5 x (45 - 5) mL x 120 mmHg = 2,400 mmHg mL
cards.section: The classic experiment: what a beat costs in oxygen

cards.front: In the linear model, stroke work peaks when Ea equals Ees. Why does efficiency (work per unit oxygen) peak at a lower Ea/Ees, and what moves that peak?
cards.back: Without the PVA-independent oxygen intercept, work per PVA only falls as Ea/Ees rises; the fixed cost creates the peak. A larger fixed cost relative to PVA moves the peak up.
cards.quote: Without the intercept, work per PVA only falls as Ea/Ees rises; the intercept, oxygen spent regardless of load, creates the peak.
cards.section: Where the efficiency peak falls

cards.front: A drug said to be a positive inotrope also dilates arterioles. In an anaesthetized dog, EF rose from 55 to 65 percent. Using a left-ventricular conductance catheter and an inferior vena cava balloon, how would you test whether contractility rose?
cards.back: EF cannot separate the effects, since afterload reduction alone raises it. Pace the heart at a fixed rate, calibrate volume, then after vehicle and after drug record steady loops and brief caval occlusions: fit Ees and V0 to the end-systolic corners, and compute Ea = Pes / SV.
cards.why: Use the first few beats before reflexes act, and fit both Ees and V0, since a V0 shift alone can mimic a slope change.
cards.quote: Afterload reduction alone raises EF (part 2 run backwards), so EF cannot separate the two effects.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: After an arteriolar-dilating drug, the end-systolic corners from caval occlusions fall on the same ESPVR as after vehicle, while Ea falls and EF rises. What do you conclude?
cards.back: The EF rise reflects loading (lower afterload, plus any change in EDV), not contractility. A steeper ESPVR after drug than after vehicle would have supported an inotropic effect.
cards.quote: If the end-systolic points before and after the drug lie on one ESPVR while Ea falls, the EF rise reflects loading, not contractility
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A left-ventricular conductance catheter reads EDV 160 mL and ESV 90 mL. A saline bolus later shows that parallel conductance adds a constant 40 mL to every reading. Compare uncorrected and corrected stroke volume and EF.
cards.back: SV = 70 mL either way, since a constant offset cancels in a difference. EF: uncorrected 70 / 160 = 44 percent; corrected 70 / 120 = 58 percent.
cards.quote: Tissue around the cavity adds a parallel conductance to its reading, a roughly constant extra volume, found by briefly changing blood conductivity with a bolus.
cards.section: The ventricle's line: a stiff line at end-systole, a soft curve at end-diastole

cards.front: The third heart sound, S3, falls in {{c1::rapid early filling}}; S4, when present, comes with atrial contraction.
cards.quote: S3 falls in rapid early filling; S4, when present, with atrial contraction.
cards.section: The Wiggers diagram in more detail
